items.description_text: About the training Write a Project, Make a Change! is an intensive and highly practical training course for people who want to learn how to transform ideas and community needs into strong Erasmus+ youth projects. During the training, participants will work in international teams and go through the main stages of developing an Erasmus+ project: identifying needs, defining objectives, designing activities, planning impact and dissemination, and drafting key parts of an application. This will not be a training based mainly on presentations. Participants will write, analyse, solve problems, give and receive feedback, develop project ideas and work on practical assignments throughout the week. Previous experience in project writing is welcome, but it is not required. We are more interested in participants' motivation, ability to learn, quality of thinking and willingness to work seriously during the course. Our objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: analyse the needs of young people and local communities and transform them into relevant project ideas; develop coherent Erasmus+ youth projects by connecting needs, objectives, activities, learning outcomes, impact and dissemination; formulate SMART and meaningful project objectives; draft and critically evaluate key sections of an Erasmus+ application; understand the main principles and quality criteria behind Erasmus+ youth projects; work effectively in international project teams; give and receive constructive feedback and improve project ideas accordingly; present and defend a project concept clearly. Who are we looking for? The training also provides opportunities to exchange good practices, explore successful initiatives from different European countries, and develop new project ideas responding to current challenges in youth participation and democratic engagement. items.description_text: Across Europe and beyond, LGBTQAI+ communities are facing increasing political pressure, shrinking civic space, and rising polarisation. These developments directly affect queer young people and the organisations and youth workers supporting them. In this context, youth work is not only a space for support and belonging, but also a site of resistance, community building, and democratic engagement. Experienced LGBTQAI+ youth workers and organisations have developed a wide range of practices – from creating brave and inclusive spaces while fostering community resilience, to implementing participatory and democratic education approaches. At the same time, many of these practices are closely connected to queer feminist and grassroots activist traditions, often without being explicitly recognised or articulated within youth work frameworks. This training course aims to create a space for experienced practitioners to come together, exchange and deepen their practices, and critically reflect on the role of queer youth work in today’s geopolitical context. Through inspirational inputs, study visits, and peer-learning processes, participants will explore how to strengthen their work, build meaningful connections, and respond to the evolving realities faced by queer young people and communities. In this call we aim for a group of approximately 20 participants. items.description_text: Aim To empower youth workers with practical knowledge, digital tools, and ethical frameworks. Objectives: Look at the big picture: To figure out where tech has been, where it is now, and how we can actually use it in everyday youth work. Keep a healthy balance: To talk about screen fatigue and make sure well-being, movement, and downtime are built right into our daily routines and project plans. items.title: Outdoor Paths: Designing Experiential Activities for Young People
items.summary: An online workshop for youth workers to design safe, inclusive outdoor learning journeys. Using visual “island–storm–harbour” maps, participants turn real group needs into structured outdoor games, reflection walks and community‑based challenges.

items.description_text: This online workshop is designed for youth workers who already use games and activities with young people and want to upgrade them into well‑designed outdoor and experiential learning processes. Instead of offering a random collection of icebreakers, the training focuses on how to: turn real issues from youth work (group tension, low participation, stress, intercultural challenges) into outdoor and experiential activities plan activities that are safe, inclusive and purposeful in very different local contexts – from small neighbourhood parks to busy city centres. Participants work with a simple “learning journey” metaphor (island – wind – storms – harbour – legacy) to map what supports and what blocks them when they plan outdoor learning with young people. Building on this, they learn a step‑by‑step planning model: Define a clear learning focus (e.g. trust, communication, dealing with uncertainty, reconnecting with nature). Choose and analyse a real space they have access to (street, park, school yard, seaside, village square). Design an activity that uses this space as a co‑facilitator: routes, objects, landmarks and people become part of the game or challenge. Prepare guiding questions for briefing, risk assessment, inclusion (who might be left out and why), and debriefing. The workshop mixes short inputs with practical design sprints in small groups. items.summary: An online workshop using simple examples and mission‑based design, participants learn how to use robots to develop teamwork, problem‑solving and creativity with young people – even with limited equipment.

items.description_text: A practical online workshop designed for youth workers, trainers and educators who want to explore educational robotics as a tool for learning. The focus is on how robots and simple programmable devices can support skills such as collaboration, planning, resilience and systems thinking. Participants explore what “robotics” can look like in youth work: from programmable toys and simple kits to low‑tech simulations of robots when no hardware is available. Through concrete examples, the session introduces the idea of mission‑based activities: small challenges where a “robot” has to achieve a goal (follow a line, move an object, navigate a map, simulate a social scenario). Participants see how each mission can be framed around real‑life issues, such as accessibility, environmental protection, or community problem‑solving, turning robotics into a vehicle for values and discussion. In groups, participants design one robotics session tailored to their own context and resources. They choose a mission, define roles within the team (e.g. programmer, builder, tester, documenter), and outline the steps from briefing to testing to debriefing. They also plan how they will handle mistakes and failures as learning moments, and how they will invite all young people to contribute, regardless of technical confidence. The workshop concludes with presentations of the session plans, peer feedback and a short reflection on how robotics can connect to broader youth work goals, such as inclusion, participation and digital literacy. By the end of the workshop, participants will: see robotics as an accessible method for youth work rather than a purely technical field understand how to frame robotics activities as missions with clear learning goals have a ready‑to‑test session plan adapted to their own level of equipment and group needs feel more prepared to use robotics to support soft skills, creativity and interest in technology among young people.

items.description_text: An experiential online lab for trainers and youth workers that combines the spirit of Ask Better, Teach Better with the creative tools of Play to Learn. The focus is on how powerful questions can be turned into interactive stories, low‑tech games and short AI‑generated video events that help young people explore complex situations in a safe, playful way. Participants start from their own practice: each small group brings one concrete issue from their work with young people (for example participation, conflict, online behaviour, inclusion, or the impact of AI). Building on this, they design a very simple branching story in 3–4 scenes, where different types of questions and choices lead to different outcomes. Groups create a simple shared space or board, define roles and a common goal, and design question cards and event cards that players draw as they move through the situation. The game is intentionally low‑tech, using materials that are easy to find in any youth setting (paper, markers, scarves, balls, simple objects), to show that meaningful game design does not require expensive equipment. These videos are used as live triggers during the game: when an AI‑video event appears, the group pauses, watches, and must first describe what they see and formulate new questions before deciding how to act in the game. items.description_text: We invite youth workers from Programme countries and Southern Mediterranean countries to take part in an international Partnership Building Activity (PBA) in Northern Portugal focused on inclusive youth work with young women, particularly those living in rural, remote or peripheral communities. Young women living in rural and peripheral areas experience unique realities that present both opportunities and challenges. Rural communities often offer strong social connections, a sense of belonging and growing spaces for community engagement, local leadership and social innovation. At the same time, young women may face barriers such as geographical isolation, limited mobility, reduced access to information, fewer educational and professional opportunities, persistent gender stereotypes and less direct access to youth services and international experiences. These factors can particularly affect young women with fewer opportunities, influencing their participation in community life and their awareness of, and access to, local, national and European opportunities. Youth work has an important role to play in recognising the strengths of rural communities while addressing the barriers that prevent young women from fully participating, accessing information and benefiting from the opportunities available to them. Youth workers and youth organisations play an important role in addressing these inequalities. They can create inclusive spaces, provide information, accompany young women in accessing opportunities and develop practices that respond to the realities of their communities. The PBA will bring together youth workers from E+ and ESC Programme and Southern Mediterranean countries to exchange experiences and reflect on how their organisations engage young women, remove barriers and make opportunities more visible, accessible and inclusive. Throughout the week, we will explore how nature can inspire educational practice, how communities can become powerful learning environments, and how non-formal education can help young people develop resilience, participation and a stronger connection with themselves, others and the natural world. Rather than focusing only on theories, we will experiment, reflect and learn together through direct experience. For example, as indicated by the YPS monitoring (Dr. Dan Moxon, YPS Steering group, 2024), between 2021 and 2023, only 9.8% of participants in Erasmus+ Youth projects with participation themes were young people with fewer opportunities (YPFO) (considerably lower than the 30% of estimated participants in Erasmus+ KA1 activities (Youth Exchanges, Youth Workers Mobility and Youth Participation activities) who are YPFO). Youth workers, educators, and trainers are key actors in supporting these young people, but they often lack practical tools and knowledge to address the specific challenges these youth face when engaging in democratic life. This study visit is part of a long-term project organised by SALTO Inclusion & Diversity and SALTO Participation & Information, which aims to strengthen competences to design and facilitate inclusive, accessible, and meaningful democratic participation processes with diverse groups of young people. items.description_text: Across Europe, democratic values are increasingly under pressure, and public discourse is becoming more polarised. Amid these developments, youth work stands at a crossroads: socially and politically relevant enough to matter yet increasingly expected to remain “apolitical” and focus on individual life skills. Youth work practitioners often find themselves navigating difficult dilemmas, such as how youth work can operate effectively in politically volatile and polarised environments, what its role is in safeguarding democracy, and whether depoliticisation is a viable response or itself a political choice. And if not, how can youth workers navigate the risks and responsibilities of taking a stand for democracy? The seminar targets youth work practitioners who want to strengthen democratic values and attitudes amongst their target group and within their communities, and exchange ideas and experiences with like-minded colleagues. In particular, the seminar aims to offer a space for youth work practitioners to: -explore the current state of democracy and better understand its implications for youth work and young people's lives; -reflect on the ethical and political dimensions of youth work and its role in promoting and sustaining democratic values; -examine existing projects, initiatives, and practices that have responded to democratic backsliding and critically reflect on what worked well and what was less effective; -enable and support participants in finding the right approach in their youth work to strengthen and support democratic values in their local context; -encourage participants to develop concrete follow-up activities for their local youth work and communities. items.title: PLAY IS HUMAN RIGHT – The neuroscience of joy and the NVC practice of connection
items.summary: Inspired by Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience and Nonviolent Communication (NVC), this webinar explores how the PLAY system supports connection, resilience, creativity, and emotional wellbeing.
items.participants_countries: Erasmus+ Youth Programme countries , Other countries in the world , Partner Countries Neighbouring the EU
items.fee_text: no
items.description_text: In Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience, PLAY is one of the brain’s primary emotional systems—a neural circuit that supports connection, flexibility, learning, resilience, and social trust. And yet, in many adult lives, especially in work, parenting, leadership, and intimate relationships, play often disappears first. During this webinar, we will explore the PLAY circuit through the lens of Nonviolent Communication (NVC). Together, we will discover why play requires a sense of safety, how joy differs from entertainment or performance, and how a playful presence can soften tension, open space for dialogue, and support our needs for connection, freedom, creativity, ease, and belonging. We will also ask: What happens to our relationships when play is absent? Why do we sometimes lose access to lightness, curiosity, and spontaneity? How can sharing NVC help us bring play back without forcing it, bypassing pain, or pretending everything is okay? Where playfulness can support sharing and learning NVC? This webinar is for people who want to understand play not as a luxury, but as a deep human need and a powerful doorway to empathy, regulation, and more alive relationships. It is a result of the Erasmus + training course “Flying Giraffes” that took place in Poland in June 2026. You can register here: https://www.fundacjamudita.org/en/play-is-human-right-the-neuroscience-of-joy-and-the-nvc-practice-of-connection-with-paulina-orbitowska-fernandez/

items.description_text: Do you sometimes feel overwhelmed by your emotions and wish you could understand them better? Would you like to respond to difficult situations with more awareness, empathy, and choice? Emotions are not something to fix, hide, or “manage away.” They are signals that tell us what matters, what hurts, what we long for, and what may need our attention. In this webinar, we will explore emotions through the lens of Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We will look at how to recognise and name feelings, listen to the needs beneath them, stay present when emotions become intense, and move from automatic reaction towards greater connection and conscious choice. IN THIS WEBINAR, YOU WILL EXPLORE: how to understand and embrace emotions with empathy; how NVC can help us recognise feelings and underlying needs; simple ways to regulate yourself in difficult moments; how to respond with more awareness and choice. The session will combine accessible theoretical input with reflection and practical tools that you can bring into everyday life and your work with others.

items.description_text: Play for Human Rights is an international training course for youth workers taking place in Dobczyce, Poland, from 23 to 31 October 2026. The project will bring together 24 youth workers from eight countries for a seven-day learning programme focused on Human Rights Education (HRE), Intercultural Learning (ICL) and democratic participation. The central methodology of the training will be an immersive, long-form role-play simulation. Through experiential learning, participants will explore human dignity, equality, discrimination, cultural diversity, democracy and civic engagement. They will learn how to design, facilitate and debrief educational simulations that foster empathy, critical thinking, intercultural dialogue and active citizenship among young people. The programme will combine practical exercises, role-play, group reflection, structured debriefing, self-assessment and collaborative design. Participants will strengthen their competences in facilitation, programme development, intercultural communication, inclusion, evaluation and safe and ethical youth-work practice, in line with the European Training Strategy Competence Model for Youth Workers. Throughout the training, participants will co-create and test at least five transferable workshops addressing human rights, discrimination, equality, diversity and democratic participation. The developed methods will be suitable for adaptation to different youth-work settings and to the needs of young people with fewer opportunities, including young people from migrant, Roma, rural and NEET backgrounds. The project will also support participating organisations in integrating simulation-based Human Rights Education and Intercultural Learning into their regular activities. After the training, participants will be expected to transfer the acquired knowledge to their local communities, organise follow-up activities and contribute to the dissemination and visibility of the project and its results. items.description_text: The first training course in the LIFT programme cycle will introduce participants to the methodology of youth work in the context of youth exchanges. It will focus on developing the competences needed to facilitate learning processes, create meaningful participation opportunities for young people, and support their personal and social development. Participants will explore how to empower young people by giving them ownership of activities, accompanying them in their learning journeys rather than directing them, and recognising the key needs of young people in this area. The programme combines experiential learning, peer exchange, reflection, and practical facilitation exercises to prepare participants for leading future international youth exchanges and contributing to high-quality youth work. The objectives for this Training Course are: - To internalise youth work methodology and strengthen the youth work approach towards young people participating in youth exchanges, - To develop facilitators’ competences, especially empowering and giving space based on identified needs, - To consolidate teams of facilitators who’ll confidently support young people in their youth exchanges, - To develop practical and tailor-made solutions on how to support young people in the development of their youth exchanges. items.description_text: Context Human rights educators, activists, and youth workers across Europe navigate an increasingly unpredictable context. Shrinking civil society spaces, systemic uncertainty, and financial instability create high-stress environments that directly impact psychological well-being. This ongoing strain often leads to professional burnout, affecting both individual educators and the long-term sustainability of youth organisations and their work. This 7-day training course offers a dedicated space for youth workers to step back, address work-related stress, build emotional resilience, and discover actionable tools to safeguard their mental well-being—and the well-being of the young people they support. We are bringing together youth workers, trainers, and activists to step off the treadmill, address the psychological weight of our work, and build practical emotional resilience. It is not about standard self-care; it’s about discovering collective, realistic tools to protect our well-being and keep our organisations sustainable while learning how to better support the young people we work with. Participants' profile The course is designed for 25 youth workers, trainers, educators, and activists involved in running human rights educational activities with young people on a regular basis. Target Regions: Programme Countries, Eastern Partnership (EaP) and Western Balkan countries. New legislation, professional standards, competence frameworks, local youth centres and innovative forms of youth participation are emerging across the region. Practitioners and policy makers face common challenges: strengthening recognition of youth work, improving quality, creating sustainable support systems, responding to societal change, and ensuring that youth work remains relevant to young people's realities. At the same time, youth workers in Eastern Europe and Caucasus are responding to challenges such as armed conflicts, democratic resilience, migration, digital transformation, shrinking civic space, mental health, social cohesion and the participation of young people in rapidly changing societies. Their experience of building resilient youth work systems under rapidly changing circumstances offers valuable lessons not only for the region itself but also for youth workers across Europe seeking to strengthen the resilience of young people, communities and youth work structures in the twenty-first century. Youth engagement is increasingly recognised as a decisive force in achieving Europe’s green transition. Both formal (school systems, civic participation structures) and informal (community projects, youth work) pathways empower young people to contribute to environmental action. The European Green Deal support initiatives emphasise that youth bring creativity, fresh perspectives, and a direct stake in long‑term climate solutions, making their involvement indispensable. The Council of Europe’s groundbreaking Recommendation on Young People and Climate Action stresses that young people must be meaningfully included in climate decision‑making processes. The recommendation highlights the need to protect young climate defenders, ensure access to rights, and remove structural barriers preventing youth from influencing policy. items.description_text: Das Training richtet sich an Fachkräfte der Jugendarbeit sowie an Entscheidungsträgerinnen und Entscheidungsträger, die sich mit der Gestaltung, Entwicklung und politischen Rahmung von Räumen für junge Menschen befassen. Ziel des Trainings ist es, neue Perspektiven auf jugendgerechte Orte zu eröffnen und innovative Modelle kennenzulernen, die Begegnung, Austausch und selbstbestimmte Nutzung ermöglichen. Ausgangspunkt bildet der in Luxemburg formulierte Bedarf junger Menschen nach frei zugänglichen, sicheren und attraktiven Orten, an denen sie sich treffen, Zeit miteinander verbringen, Erlebnisse teilen und Erfahrungen sammeln können. Das Training greift diesen Bedarf auf und lädt dazu ein, das Angebot an Räumen für Jugendliche neu zu denken und weiterzuentwickeln. Im Rahmen des Trainings werden europäische Praxisbeispiele aus Belgien, Südtirol, der Schweiz und Deutschland vorgestellt. Sie zeigen, wie Räume für junge Menschen in unterschiedlichen Kontexten gestaltet und betrieben werden können. Ergänzend werden die luxemburgischen Rahmenbedingungen beleuchtet. Die Teilnehmenden haben die Möglichkeit, sich mit Vertreterinnen und Vertretern der vorgestellten Organisationen auszutauschen und Einblicke in deren Arbeitsweisen, Herausforderungen und Erfolgsfaktoren zu gewinnen. Ein weiterer Programmpunkt ist die Besichtigung eines vom nationalen Jugenddienst geführten Maker Space. Die Teilnehmenden lernen vor Ort ein konkretes Praxisbeispiel kennen und können sich mit den verantwortlichen Fachkräften austauschen. Das Training bietet Raum für Reflexion, Diskussion und Vernetzung. Es unterstützt die Teilnehmenden dabei, neue Ansätze kennenzulernen und Anregungen für die eigene Praxis mitzunehmen. Ziel ist es, Impulse für die Weiterentwicklung jugendgerechter Räume in Europa zu setzen und Angebote nachhaltig an den Bedürfnissen junger Menschen auszurichten.

items.description_text: This course explores how youth work can become genuinely inclusive — moving beyond a declarative discourse on diversity towards everyday practice. Starting from the participants' own experience, we examine the common pitfalls that organisations, programmes and facilitators fall into (tokenism, surface-level or performative inclusion, assuming a space is neutral, one-size-fits-all approaches, accessibility treated as an afterthought, unconscious bias in recruitment and facilitation) and we build concrete solutions for designing learning and growth environments that value diversity. Do you want to explore the opportunities of the Erasmus+ Programme? Then “Dive into Youth Participation” is the Training Course for you! Youth participation in democratic life and young people's active civic engagement are high priorities of the EU Youth Strategy and are incorporated into the majority of contemporary youth policy frameworks in different European countries. The Erasmus+ Programme is one of the mechanisms to put the EU Youth Strategy into practice and provide many opportunities for young people to develop international projects, which empower them to take an active role in society and help them develop civic and social competencies. In this context, the fourth edition of the Training Course “Dive into Youth Participation” brings together 25 youth leaders and youth workers from different European countries with an aim to improve their understanding and practices toward quality youth participation. items.description_text: NGO Awero team, Nexes Interculturals, Cities of Learning Network partners, and the International Youth Work Trainers Guild are offering a 6th modular training for trainers, aligned to the European Training Strategy (ETS) competence model. The training course will contribute to the development of the ETS trainers’ competences in the area of “Being Civically Engaged”. Understanding and asserting the trainer's work as an act of civic engagement Connecting relevant [youth] policies and educational programmes to own values, beliefs and different political perspectives Reflecting on personal civic engagement, values and beliefs, and integrating them in the training practice in a responsible and constructive way Supporting learners in developing critical thinking and using the diversity of opinions and beliefs as a source of learning Applying democracy and human rights principles in the design and delivery of training activities. Midweek, the group will travel to Barcelona to explore civic engagement and local training practices, including a Migrantour optional session in one of Barcelona’s neighbourhoods. The later days shift to developing pilot civically engaged training practice ideas, examining diversity, democracy and human rights as sources of learning, and covering resources for trainers' professional development and recognition. items.description_text: Why this programme? Young people increasingly experience the world through digital, visual, interactive and participatory media. At the same time, heritage education can sometimes remain centred on traditional formats: guided tours, exhibitions, historical information and passive observation. This creates an opportunity for youth work. New media can provide alternative entry points into heritage, allowing young people to: explore places and stories through immersive experiences; discover hidden or forgotten narratives; connect personal and community memories with wider European heritage; question dominant interpretations of history; create their own narratives; collaborate across cultures; transform physical spaces into interactive learning environments. The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. Specific objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Explore contemporary approaches to cultural heritage and heritage awareness. Identify opportunities for using immersive and interactive media in youth work. Experiment with VR, AR, 360° media, projection mapping, interactive installations, digital storytelling and other creative technologies. Design non-formal education activities connecting young people with local, national and European heritage. Use storytelling and participatory methodologies to make heritage more relevant to young people. Encourage young people to question, reinterpret and remix heritage narratives. items.description_text: How can international youth mobility become truly safe, inclusive, and empowering for Highly Vulnerable Young People? A course for youth workers, facilitators, and organisations to learn how to create safer, more inclusive, and trauma-informed international mobility experiences for Highly Vulnerable Young People (HVYP). This is a self-paced and practice-oriented online course for professionals working in youth mobility and non-formal education. The course supports participants in developing the competencies needed to responsibly include and support young people facing multiple and intersecting barriers in international programmes. You are going to learn about: safer and more inclusive mobility environments, safeguarding and risk management in practice, trauma-informed and solution-focused approaches, recognising and preventing harm and exclusion, supporting HVYP before, during, and after mobility experiences, professional boundaries, crisis response, and self-care in youth work. About this course International youth mobility projects can create powerful opportunities for learning, participation, connection, and personal growth. At the same time, for highly vulnerable young people, unfamiliar international environments may also involve increased vulnerability and risk. This course was developed within the LADDER project to support youth workers and organisations in creating mobility experiences that are not only accessible, but genuinely safe, supportive, and empowering. Through practical examples, case studies, reflection exercises, and field-tested approaches, participants will strengthen their capacity to: create safer and more inclusive mobility projects, anticipate and prevent risks, respond responsibly to challenging situations, and support young people facing multiple barriers. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition. The event will take place outdoors and is aimed at educators, activity leaders, and facilitators. In Brittany, 27 participants are expected.
